name: Infrastructure as Code
description: Terraform, state, drift, modules and configuration management — infrastructure you can review, test and rebuild.

modules.name: Principles & Terraform
modules.description: Declarative infrastructure, state, and the workflow that keeps it safe.

cards.prompt: What does infrastructure as code give you over clicking in a console?
cards.answer: Reviewable changes, version history, reproducibility across environments, drift detection, disaster recovery by re-apply, and documentation that cannot go stale because it *is* the infrastructure.
cards.explanation: The pivotal property is reproducibility: you can stand up an identical staging environment, or rebuild after a region failure, because the definition is complete. Console clicking produces snowflakes nobody can recreate — including the person who made them.

resources.title: HashiCorp — What is infrastructure as code?

cards.answer: Declarative describes the desired end state and lets the tool compute the diff; imperative runs the steps you write to get there.

left.title: Declarative (Terraform, CFN, K8s)
points: Plan shows the diff before applying
Awkward for genuine sequences and one-offs

right.title: Imperative (scripts, CLI, SDK)
points: Easy to reason about step by step

cards.explanation: Ansible sits between: declarative-ish tasks executed in order. Use declarative for resources that persist and imperative for actions that happen once. The mistake is scripting `aws create-*` calls and calling it IaC — there is no reconciliation.

cards.prompt: What is Terraform state, and why does it need care?
cards.answer: A mapping from your configuration to real resource ids, plus cached attributes. It is how Terraform knows what it already created. It must be stored remotely, locked during apply, versioned, and treated as sensitive — it can contain secrets in plaintext.
cards.explanation: Two people applying against local state produces duplicated or destroyed resources; that is what state locking (DynamoDB, blob leases) prevents. `terraform import` adopts existing resources, and `state mv` handles refactors — never hand-edit the file.

cards.prompt: Someone fixed an incident by changing a security group in the console. What happens on the next apply, and what should the team do?
cards.answer: Terraform sees drift and reverts the manual change — potentially re-breaking production. The fix is to reconcile deliberately: bring the change into code, then apply. Prevent recurrence by restricting console write access and running drift detection on a schedule.
cards.explanation: Emergency console changes are sometimes correct — the failure is not writing them back. A scheduled `terraform plan` that alerts on any diff turns silent drift into a visible task while the reasoning is still fresh.

cards.prompt: How should you structure IaC across environments?
cards.answer: Reusable modules with input variables, composed by thin per-environment root configurations with separate state. Environments differ by variable values (sizes, counts, CIDRs), not by copied code.
cards.explanation: Separate state per environment limits blast radius — a bad apply cannot touch production. Resist over-abstracting early: a module with thirty variables and conditional logic is harder to follow than two explicit files.

modules.name: Operating IaC
modules.description: Review, testing, secrets and the day-two realities.

cards.prompt: What should stop this plan from being applied?
cards.answer: A forced replacement of the primary database — that destroys and recreates it, losing data and causing an outage. Investigate why the attribute forces replacement and use an in-place upgrade path instead.
cards.explanation: Always read the plan, especially the destroy count and any `forces replacement` comment. `prevent_destroy` on stateful resources turns a catastrophic apply into an error. Requiring plan output in the pull request makes this reviewable by someone other than the author.

cards.prompt: What is policy as code, and where does it run?
cards.answer: Machine-enforced rules — no public S3 buckets, encryption required, mandatory tags — evaluated against the plan in CI (Checkov, tfsec, OPA/Conftest, Sentinel) and again at the cloud control plane (SCPs, Azure Policy).
cards.explanation: Catching it in the pull request is cheap and educational; catching it at the control plane is the guarantee. You want both, because IaC is not the only way resources get created.

cards.prompt: How do you handle a database password in Terraform?
cards.answer: Do not put it in the configuration or in a tfvars file. Generate it with a random resource or reference a secret manager, and let the application read it at runtime. Remember the value still lands in state, so state must be encrypted and access-controlled.
cards.explanation: 'It is in a private repo' is not protection — repos get cloned, forked and leaked. The cleanest pattern is Terraform creating an empty secret container and a separate process populating it, so the value never enters the IaC path at all.

cards.prompt: What is immutable infrastructure, and what does it replace?
cards.answer: Servers are never modified in place — a change means building a new image and replacing the instance. It replaces configuration management that mutates long-lived servers, and with it, configuration drift.
cards.explanation: Immutability makes rollback trivial (deploy the previous image) and eliminates the 'works on that box' problem. It requires externalised state, quick image builds and automated replacement — which is exactly what containers and autoscaling groups provide.

modules.name: Terraform Mechanics
modules.description: The core workflow, providers and lifecycles, variables and outputs, data sources, count versus for_each, and importing.

cards.prompt: What do `terraform init`, `plan` and `apply` each do?
cards.answer: `init` downloads providers and modules and configures the state backend; `plan` compares configuration, state and real infrastructure and shows the proposed changes; `apply` executes a plan (ideally a saved plan file from `plan -out`).
cards.explanation: Applying a saved plan guarantees you get exactly what was reviewed, not a fresh plan computed minutes later against changed infrastructure. `terraform fmt` and `validate` belong in CI alongside a plan whose output is posted to the pull request.

cards.prompt: What do the `lifecycle` settings `prevent_destroy`, `create_before_destroy` and `ignore_changes` do?
cards.answer: `prevent_destroy` makes any plan that would destroy the resource an error — for databases and buckets. `create_before_destroy` builds the replacement before removing the old one, avoiding downtime on forced replacement. `ignore_changes` stops Terraform reverting attributes managed elsewhere (for example an autoscaler's desired count).
cards.explanation: These encode operational intent that the provider cannot know. Overusing `ignore_changes` hides real drift, so scope it to specific attributes and comment why.

cards.prompt: What are input variables, locals and outputs in Terraform?
cards.answer: Input variables are a module's parameters (with types, defaults, descriptions and validation rules). Locals are named intermediate expressions inside a module. Outputs expose values — IDs, endpoints — to the calling module or to other configurations.
cards.explanation: Type and validate variables so mistakes fail at plan time. Mark secrets `sensitive = true` to keep them out of plan output (they still land in state). Treat outputs as a module's public API: renaming one breaks every consumer.

cards.prompt: What is a data source, and how does it differ from a resource?
cards.answer: A data source reads information about something that exists — an AMI ID, an existing VPC, the current account — without managing it. A resource is created, updated and destroyed by this configuration and tracked in its state.
cards.explanation: Data sources connect configurations without sharing state: one stack creates the network, another looks it up by tag. They are read at plan time, so an unstable lookup (such as "latest image") can make plans change without any code change — pin where reproducibility matters.

cards.prompt: Removing `"staging"` from the middle of this list causes Terraform to destroy and recreate `prod`. Why, and what fixes it?
cards.answer: `count` addresses instances by index, so removing an element shifts every later index: `bucket[1]` becomes what was `bucket[2]`, and Terraform sees changes it must apply by replacement. `for_each` over a set or map keys each instance by a stable key (`bucket["prod"]`), so removing one leaves the rest untouched.
cards.explanation: Use `count` only for identical copies or as an on/off switch (`count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0`). When refactoring from `count` to `for_each`, add `moved` blocks so existing resources are re-addressed instead of recreated.

cards.prompt: How do you bring existing resources under Terraform, and refactor addresses without destroying anything?
cards.answer: Use `import` blocks (or `terraform import`) to adopt a resource into state, then write the matching configuration until the plan shows no changes. Use `moved` blocks to rename resources or move them into modules, so Terraform updates addresses instead of destroying and recreating.
cards.explanation: Both are declarative and reviewable in a pull request, unlike manual `terraform state` commands. `terraform plan -generate-config-out` can draft configuration for imported resources as a starting point.

resources.title: Terraform docs — Refactoring with moved blocks

modules.name: Beyond Terraform
modules.description: Configuration management, general-purpose-language IaC, testing infrastructure code and structuring environments.

cards.answer: Provisioning tools create and manage infrastructure resources through cloud APIs — networks, VMs, databases. Configuration management configures what runs inside machines — packages, files, users, services — usually over SSH or an agent.
cards.explanation: With immutable images and containers, much configuration moves into image builds (Packer, Dockerfiles) and configuration management shrinks. Ansible tasks must be written idempotently — declare state (`state: present`) instead of running raw commands — so a second run changes nothing.

cards.prompt: HCL (Terraform, OpenTofu) vs general-purpose-language IaC (Pulumi, AWS CDK)
cards.answer: HCL is a constrained, declarative configuration language; Pulumi and CDK let you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go or C# with loops, functions, classes and package managers, while still producing a declarative plan.
cards.explanation: Real languages help build reusable abstractions and test them with normal test frameworks, but invite cleverness that makes infrastructure hard to review. HCL's limits keep configurations readable by operators. Either works — consistency and review quality matter more than the choice.

cards.prompt: How do you test infrastructure code?
cards.answer: Layers: formatting and validation (`fmt`, `validate`, tflint), static policy and security scanning of the plan (Checkov, OPA), unit-style tests of module logic (`terraform test` with mocked providers), and integration tests that apply to a sandbox account and assert on real resources before tearing them down (terraform test, Terratest).
cards.explanation: Most value comes cheaply from linting, policy checks and reviewing plans in pull requests. Full apply-and-destroy tests are slow and cost money, so reserve them for shared modules many teams depend on.

cards.prompt: Terraform workspaces vs a separate directory (root module) per environment
cards.answer: Workspaces reuse one configuration with multiple state files, selected by name; per-environment directories give each environment its own small root module, backend and variables, all calling shared modules.

left.title: Workspaces
points: Easy to target the wrong one

right.title: Directory per environment
points: A root module per env calling shared modules

cards.explanation: Workspaces make it easy to apply to the wrong environment and hard to vary structure between environments. Separate roots are more explicit and allow different backends, credentials and review rules for production. Workspaces fit short-lived copies of the same stack, such as per-branch test environments.
